rationale: C01 plausibly supplied substantial language and argumentative machinery for the child. Both are replies to a Soviet chairman that open by affirming the American commitment to peace, reject Soviet allegations that American defensive action endangers peace, invoke the failure of appeasement in the 1930s, place primary responsibility for urgent threats in the United Nations Security Council, criticize Soviet vetoes, and condition a summit meeting on adequate diplomatic preparation. The child adapts this framework to the Lebanon crisis and even updates C01's count of Soviet vetoes from 82 to 85. C14 and C25 contain related summit-preparation arguments, but neither matches the child's combined peace, Security Council, veto, and summit structure as fully as C01.

shared_material.child_excerpt: May I assure you that the establishment and maintenance of a just peace is the dominant influence in American policy.
shared_material.parent_excerpt: I can assure you, Mr. Chairman, that in the United States the waging of peace has priority in every aspect, and every element, of our national life.
shared_material.explanation: Closely parallel opening assurances that peace governs American policy.

shared_material.child_excerpt: We do not want to see a repetition of the progressive destruction of the independence of small nations which occurred during the 1930's and which led to the Second World War. To be acquiescent in aggression...is not the road to peace.
shared_material.parent_excerpt: Three times in this century wars have occurred under circumstances which strongly suggest...that war would not have occurred had the United States been militarily strong and committed in advance to the defense of nations that were attacked.
shared_material.explanation: Both use the historical failure to resist aggression as the central rebuttal to the Soviet claim that collective defense threatens peace.

shared_material.child_excerpt: By Article 24 of the United Nations Charter, the Soviet Union, with other members of the United Nations, has conferred on the Security Council 'primary responsibility for the maintenance of international peace and security.'
shared_material.parent_excerpt: our two governments and others signed the Charter of the United Nations, conferring upon its Security Council primary responsibility for the maintenance of international peace and security.
shared_material.explanation: Distinctive shared Charter-based formulation assigning primary peacekeeping responsibility to the Security Council.

shared_material.child_excerpt: The Soviet Union, by its constant abuse of its veto power in the Security Council--its veto of today was the 85th--would tear down, and not strengthen, the orderly processes
shared_material.parent_excerpt: The Soviet Union has persistently prevented the establishment of such a universal collective security system and has, by its use of the veto--now 82 times--made the Security Council undependable as a protector of the peace.
shared_material.explanation: Highly specific repeated device: criticizing Soviet obstruction through an updated running count of Security Council vetoes.

shared_material.child_excerpt: I cannot but deplore the persistent refusal of your Government for so many months to agree to the adequate preparation of a 'summit' meeting
shared_material.parent_excerpt: Preparatory work, with good will on both sides, is a prerequisite to success...It would be essential that prior to such a meeting these complex matters should be worked on in advance through diplomatic channels and by our Foreign Ministers
shared_material.explanation: The child reuses C01's substantive condition that summit diplomacy requires prior preparation through regular diplomatic channels.
